word:lxx:L700026.explanation: Abdedom is a personal name, also rendered “Avthethom.” It identifies a person rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs 12 times across 10 verses, almost entirely in 1 Chronicles, with one occurrence in 2 Chronicles. Its meaning as a name is not further defined by the available lexical information, so the name itself is the supported sense. The precise role of the person in any particular verse requires that verse’s surrounding context.

word:lxx:L700053.explanation: Abi is a personal name. Abi is identified as Joab’s son. He is also identified as a commander-in-chief.

word:lxx:L700134.explanation: Angai, also given as Angge, is a proper name in the Greek Old Testament (LXX). Its meaning is not an ordinary descriptive idea such as an action, quality, or object; it functions as a specific name. The form occurs four times in this corpus, in Genesis 12:8, Genesis 13:3, and Isaiah 10:28–29. Without the surrounding verse text, its precise referent cannot be identified more specifically here.

word:lxx:L700181.explanation: This adjective means "unknown": something not known, recognized, or familiar. It describes a person, thing, or matter whose identity or nature has not been discovered or understood. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs four times, in Wisdom and 2 Maccabees. Its basic sense remains focused on the absence of knowledge or recognition; the surrounding sentence determines exactly what is unknown in each use.

word:lxx:L700211.explanation: Agōn means a contest or contention.

word:lxx:L700268.explanation: Adiel is a personal name, also rendered Athil. It identifies an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or general object. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in 1 Chronicles 9:12. The available lexical information preserves the name forms but does not provide a further descriptive meaning, so its ordinary sense is simply the person’s name. The exact significance of that individual in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700332.explanation: Azeni is a proper name used to identify someone or something named Azeni. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears twice, both times in Numbers 26:25. The available wording gives the name itself but does not provide a separate descriptive meaning or explain whether it identifies a person, family, or another named group. Its precise reference therefore depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L700439.explanation: Ailōth, also rendered Eloth, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or relationship. It identifies a named person, place, or other entity in the biblical account, but the supplied material does not include enough verse text to specify which kind of entity it names. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 2 Kings 14:22. Its precise significance there must therefore be understood from the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L700475.explanation: Aisan, also rendered Esan, is a personal name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at 1 Chronicles 4:32. Because names primarily identify people, places, or families, its meaning is best understood as the identity of the person it names, not as a general concept to apply elsewhere. The available information does not provide a separate definition beyond the name itself.

word:lxx:L700664.explanation: This noun refers to a sea-eagle or osprey, a bird identified by name in the Greek Old Testament. It occurs twice in the Septuagint, once in Leviticus and once in Deuteronomy, in lists of birds. The wording points to the bird itself rather than to an action or quality. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding list and verse context.

word:lxx:L700710.explanation: Alloni is a personal name, rendered “Allōni” or “Alloni.” It identifies an individual rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, in Numbers 26:22. Because the surrounding verse text is not included here, the name itself does not provide further information about the person or the role he has in that passage. Its meaning is therefore best understood as the proper name Alloni.

word:lxx:L700912.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means to shoot up or grow again. It describes renewed growth, like something sprouting upward after having been cut back, damaged, or previously grown. As a verb, it expresses the act or process of coming up and growing anew rather than merely possessing new life. It occurs twice in the Greek LXX, both times in Job, so its basic meaning is clear even though the surrounding verse text is not included here.

word:lxx:L701137.explanation: Aneu means without, indicating that something is absent.

word:lxx:L701195.explanation: “Lawlessly” describes an action done without regard for law or lawful order. As an adverb, it tells how someone acts rather than naming a person or thing. In the Greek LXX corpus, this word occurs once, at 2 Maccabees 8:17. Its basic sense is clear from the direct definition, while the surrounding verse determines the specific action or situation being described there.

word:lxx:L701205.explanation: This verb means “in conflict”: it describes being engaged in opposition or struggle against someone or something. As a verb, it expresses an active state of contending rather than a person, object, or abstract quality. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, in 4 Maccabees 17:14. The word’s precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its central sense is clear: being in conflict.

word:lxx:L701249.explanation: This Greek Old Testament noun means “controversy,” referring to a matter of dispute between parties. It names the disagreement itself rather than an action or a person. The word occurs 20 times in the Greek Old Testament, across 19 verses, showing that it is used repeatedly for contested matters. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L701331.explanation: This noun means “demanding back”—the act of requiring something to be returned or repaid. It describes a claim made to recover what is owed, rather than simply asking for something for the first time. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek Jewish writings represented here, it occurs seven times, including passages in Nehemiah, Zephaniah, Sirach, and 2 Maccabees. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on what is being demanded and the surrounding sentence.

word:lxx:L701348.explanation: Apantēsis means an encounter or meeting.

word:lxx:L701384.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “drive away”: to cause someone or something to leave or be sent away. It describes an action of removing or forcing away rather than simply noticing departure. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament and related deuterocanonical writings represented here, appearing once each in 1 Samuel, Ezekiel, and Wisdom. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what or whom the surrounding passage says is being driven away.

word:lxx:L701414.explanation: This adjective means “unaffected,” describing someone or something not altered or moved by an outside influence. It occurs once in the Greek Old Testament, at Genesis 25:27. Because the verse text and surrounding passage are not included here, the precise aspect of being unaffected must be understood from that passage’s context. Its basic sense remains clear: it identifies a person or thing that has not been changed, disturbed, or influenced in the relevant situation.

word:lxx:L701533.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “wash off”: it describes removing something by washing it away. It is an action word, focusing on cleansing or getting something off rather than simply becoming clean. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament represented here, in 1 Kings 22:38 and Proverbs 30:12, 20. Its precise force in any one passage depends on the surrounding verse and context.

word:lxx:L701546.explanation: This verb means “fall from”: to move downward away from a place, position, or source. It describes separation through falling rather than simply being low or falling in place. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs eight times across eight verses, including passages from Leviticus, Job, and Psalms. The exact object or circumstance involved depends on the surrounding verse, but the central idea remains a falling away or down from something.

word:lxx:L701689.explanation: Arari is a proper name, referring to a person rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. Its meaning is presented simply as “Arari,” so Scripture does not provide a broader ordinary-language definition for it. In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs three times, all in 1 Chronicles 11:34, 1 Chronicles 11:35, and 1 Chronicles 11:44. The surrounding verse text would be needed to explain each individual reference, but the word itself functions as a personal name.

word:lxx:L701780.explanation: Arnaphar, also rendered Arnafar, is a proper name referring to an individual rather than a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 7:36. The available wording preserves the name itself but does not provide a separate definition or description of the person. Its precise significance in that verse therefore depends on the surrounding genealogy and passage context.

word:lxx:L701920.explanation: Asennaios, also rendered Asenneos, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. The name itself does not provide further meaning or explain the person’s role; those details must come from the surrounding passage and its wider scriptural context.

word:lxx:L702015.explanation: This adverb means acting “honourably; honestly”—in a way marked by integrity, proper conduct, and truthfulness. Its precise force in that sentence depends on the surrounding verse and passage, but its basic sense is conduct that is upright and sincere.

word:lxx:L702059.explanation: Asōb, also rendered Asov, is a proper name rather than a word describing an action, quality, or object. Because the passage text is not included here, the name’s particular role in that verse cannot be described further. Its central meaning is therefore its function as a personal name: Asōb or Asov.

word:lxx:L702136.explanation: Aularchia means the function of a chief of the court.

word:lxx:L702143.explanation: Aunan, also rendered Avnan, is a proper name belonging to a person in the Greek Old Testament. It identifies individuals rather than expressing an action, quality, object, or relationship. The name appears ten times across eight verses, chiefly in Genesis, and also in Numbers and 1 Chronicles. Because it is a personal name, its meaning here is its identifying use: naming Aunan within genealogical and narrative passages. The surrounding verse is needed to distinguish which occurrence and person is intended.

word:lxx:L702204.explanation: This noun means “tale” or “narrative,” referring to a communicated account or story. It names the account itself rather than an action or quality. In the LXX corpus represented here, it occurs only once, in 4 Maccabees 14:6. The surrounding verse text is not included, so the word’s precise role in that passage cannot be described further; its central meaning remains an account or story.

word:lxx:L702499.explanation: “Bamōthbaal” or “Vamothvaal” is a proper name, not a general word describing an action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it appears once, at Joshua 13:17. The available information identifies the name and its two listed forms, but does not provide the verse text or a broader set of uses. Therefore, its precise significance beyond functioning as a named designation cannot be stated here.

word:lxx:L702583.explanation: This word refers to a kind of serpent, commonly rendered “basilisk.” It can function as a noun for the creature itself or as an adjective describing something associated with such a serpent. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice: once in Psalms 90:13 and once in Isaiah 59:5. The word identifies a particular serpent rather than expressing a general term for every snake; its precise force in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L702600.explanation: Baux is a proper name, referring to a person named “Baux” (also rendered “Vafks”). It appears once in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis 22:21. Because it is a personal name rather than a descriptive word, its meaning is primarily identification: it tells the reader who is being named, not what quality, action, or idea is being expressed. The surrounding verse supplies the person’s specific place in the passage.

word:lxx:L702709.explanation: This is a proper name, represented as “Bērōthaiou” or “Virotheu.” It identifies a particular person, place, or associated designation rather than describing a general action, quality, or object. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs three times, all within 2 Samuel 4. Because the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the specific referent cannot be identified more precisely from the name alone.

word:lxx:L702886.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Gazaios” or “Gazeos.” It identifies a named person or group in the Greek Old Testament rather than expressing an action, quality, or general object. word:lxx:L702918.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Gaiphaēl” or “Yefel.” It identifies a specific named entity rather than expressing a general idea, action, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Joshua 19:14. Because the available information does not include the verse text or surrounding context, the name’s particular referent cannot be identified more precisely here. Its normal function is simply to designate that named entity in the passage.

word:lxx:L703027.explanation: This noun means “jesting,” referring to speech or behavior intended as humor, teasing, or mockery. It names the act or manner of making light remarks rather than describing a person. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Jeremiah 31:27. Its precise force in that passage depends on the surrounding verse and context, but the word itself points to joking or derisive expression.

word:lxx:L703140.explanation: Gnōstēs means a knower, one who knows. It can describe someone who knows what another person has done.

word:lxx:L703298.explanation: This noun refers to a creature identified as “rough-foot.” In the Greek Old Testament, it appears only twice, once in Leviticus 11:5 and once in Deuteronomy 14:7. Its wording describes the creature by a notable physical feature rather than expressing an action, quality, or relationship. The precise significance of the term in either verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic lexical sense remains a creature characterized by a rough foot.

word:lxx:L703306.explanation: Deberi is a proper name, referring to a specific person rather than describing an action, quality, or object. It is rendered as “Deberi” and is also identified as “Theveri.” In the Greek Old Testament, this name occurs once, at 1 Chronicles 6:57. Since the verse text and surrounding context are not included here, the name’s particular role in that passage cannot be described further; its supported lexical function is simply a personal name.

word:lxx:L703373.explanation: This noun means “warden,” referring to a person responsible for guarding prisoners or overseeing a prison. It identifies an official whose duty is connected with custody and supervision, rather than describing a prisoner or a place. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Genesis 40:3. Its precise role in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its basic meaning remains a prison warden or keeper.

word:lxx:L703423.explanation: “Penetrate” means to enter through or pass into something. As a verb, this word describes an action of breaking through or making one’s way into a place or barrier. In the Greek Old Testament (LXX), it occurs once, in Numbers 14:44. The word’s basic sense remains focused on entry by passing through, while the precise force of that action in the verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L703579.explanation: Diaskorpizō means to disperse. It can describe people being dispersed among different nations rather than gathered in one place.

word:lxx:L703597.explanation: This verb means to “overturn utterly,” expressing the complete overthrow or ruin of something rather than a minor change. As a verb, it describes an action that leaves what was established decisively brought down. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs once, at 3 Maccabees 5:12. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly what is being overturned there, but the word itself points to thorough and decisive overthrow.

word:lxx:L703621.explanation: This verb means “dawn”: it describes day beginning as morning light appears. In the Greek Old Testament, it is used four times, each in a different verse, to express the arrival of dawn or the passing from night toward daylight. Its basic sense is temporal and descriptive, pointing to the beginning of the day rather than to a person, object, or action performed by someone. The precise force in any verse depends on its surrounding context.

word:lxx:L703658.explanation: διεκβολή is a noun meaning “passing through.” It refers to movement through or across a place, route, or boundary, with attention to the passage itself rather than to a person or object making it. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, appearing in Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Obadiah, and Zechariah. Its exact force in any verse depends on the surrounding wording, but its central idea remains passage from one side or point through to another.

word:lxx:L703874.explanation: Dystokeō means to be in hard labor.

word:lxx:L703957.explanation: Enkainiois means a feast of rededication.

word:lxx:L704013.explanation: This noun means a “dagger” or “handknife,” referring to a small handheld blade. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs six times, in six verses, including passages in Exodus, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and the Epistle of Jeremiah. Its basic meaning remains concrete and practical: a short knife or dagger used as an implement or weapon. The surrounding verse determines the particular use, but the word itself points to the blade rather than to an action or abstract idea.

word:lxx:L704066.explanation: This noun means “father of the nation” or “father of our nation.” It describes a person viewed as the paternal founder, ancestor, or honored father of a people. The wording can express national identity and respect, rather than merely referring to someone’s role as a biological parent. In the Greek LXX corpus, it occurs once, at 4 Maccabees 16:20; the surrounding verse is needed to determine its precise force there.

word:lxx:L704138.explanation: This adjective means “hundredfold”: something multiplied or increased by a hundred. It describes the degree or amount of something rather than naming an object by itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, once in 2 Samuel 24:3 and once in 1 Chronicles 21:3. Those references identify its two occurrences, while the surrounding verse text is needed to determine exactly what is described as hundredfold in each passage.

word:lxx:L704141.explanation: This word means “hundred,” referring to a quantity of one hundred. It is a noun used in the Greek Old Testament when counting people or groups by hundreds. The word occurs three times in the Greek Old Testament, appearing in passages from 1 Samuel, 2 Samuel, and 1 Chronicles. Its basic meaning remains numerical: it identifies a group or amount consisting of one hundred, with the surrounding verse supplying the specific people or things being counted.

word:lxx:L704220.explanation: Ekklīnō means to deviate or turn aside. It can also mean to avoid.

word:lxx:L704369.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “angry; incensed,” describing a person who has become strongly angered. It expresses an active emotional response rather than a calm judgment or mild displeasure. The word occurs once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 3 Maccabees 3:1. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding passage, but its ordinary meaning is clear: to become deeply angry or stirred with indignation.

word:lxx:L704387.explanation: This Greek Old Testament verb means “make less” or describes being “in need.” It expresses reduction—making something smaller, fewer, or diminished—or a condition in which something is lacking. The word appears three times in the Greek Old Testament, in Genesis and Psalms. Its exact force in any particular verse depends on what is being reduced or what kind of need the surrounding passage describes.

word:lxx:L704592.explanation: Empiplēmi means to fill or fill up.

word:lxx:L704602.explanation: “Spout” describes an action that sends something outward. It functions as a verb, focusing on the act itself rather than naming a person, object, or quality. In the Greek LXX, this word occurs only once, in Wisdom 15:11. Its central sense is therefore a forceful outward release, while the exact thing being released must be understood from the surrounding verse. This is a rare word in this corpus and should not be broadened into a general term for every kind of speaking, flowing, or expressing.

word:lxx:L704747.explanation: This word means “some,” referring to part of a group rather than everyone in it. It is an adjective that identifies an unspecified number or selection of people or things. In the Greek LXX material represented here, it occurs twice, both times in 3 Maccabees. The word’s basic sense remains intentionally general: it points to certain members of a larger group without naming exactly which ones or how many. Its precise reference in each passage depends on the surrounding sentence and context.

word:lxx:L704831.explanation: Exagoreuō means to tell out or make known. It is used for making confession of sin.

word:lxx:L704848.explanation: This word means “six hundredth,” identifying something by its position as number 600 in an ordered sequence. It is an adjective, so it describes a person, thing, or time associated with that ordinal number rather than naming the number six hundred itself. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, both times in Genesis, at Genesis 7:11 and Genesis 8:13. The surrounding verse determines exactly what is being identified as six hundredth.

word:lxx:L704884.explanation: This verb means to become or be “utterly weak,” describing a condition of complete loss of strength. It points to more than ordinary tiredness: the person or thing is greatly weakened and unable to remain strong. In the Greek Old Testament, this word occurs once, in Psalm 63:9. Its precise force in that verse depends on the surrounding sentence and passage, but its basic meaning is complete weakness.

word:lxx:L704905.explanation: Exereunaō means to fully explore or search out thoroughly.

word:lxx:L705083.explanation: This Greek LXX verb means “impose” or “cast on”: it describes putting something onto someone or something, or laying a matter upon them. Depending on the sentence, it can refer to placing a physical object, applying a burden, or assigning something. It occurs 66 times in the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings represented in this corpus, so its exact force is determined by the surrounding words. Its basic idea remains an action of putting or laying something upon another.

word:lxx:L705177.explanation: Epikratēsis means victory over, as in deliverance from those who attacked.

word:lxx:L705199.explanation: Epimeleomai means to care for or take care of.

word:lxx:L705209.explanation: This noun refers to the upper millstone—the stone used at a mill to grind grain. It can also describe something located at the mill. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs twice, in Deuteronomy and Judges, and both occurrences concern a millstone. The word therefore names a specific working stone rather than a general tool or place. Its precise significance in either passage depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L705300.explanation: This adjective means “necessities,” referring to what is needed or required. It functions as a describing word, pointing to necessary things rather than naming an action, person, or place. In the Greek LXX corpus represented here, it occurs nine times across 1 Chronicles, Wisdom, and the Maccabean books. Its basic sense remains focused on needs or necessary provisions; the surrounding verse determines exactly what necessities are being discussed.

word:lxx:L705436.explanation: This word is a proper name rendered “Hermōn” or “Ermon,” referring to a named biblical entity rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. In the Greek Old Testament and related Greek writings, it occurs 12 times. Its appearances are concentrated in 3 Maccabees, with additional occurrences in Judges, Psalms, and Song of Songs. The exact significance of the name in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L705443.explanation: This verb means to dye something red or make it scarlet. It describes an action involving the application or production of a red color, rather than naming the color as a mere object. In the Greek LXX, it occurs once, in Wisdom 13:14. The basic sense remains focused on coloring something red; the precise role of the verb in that verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L705515.explanation: This noun refers to something baked over a fire. It names a prepared food item rather than an action, person, or quality. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, at 2 Samuel 6:19. The word’s basic sense is specific and concrete: food made by baking over fire. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the verse’s wording.

word:lxx:L705652.explanation: This Greek LXX noun refers to a good journey or to wishes for someone’s journey to go well. It describes the idea of a favorable, successful passage from one place to another, and it can also express a spoken or wished blessing for that journey. The word occurs four times in the Greek LXX corpus, appearing once in Proverbs and three times in Sirach. Its precise force in any particular verse depends on the surrounding passage.

word:lxx:L705704.explanation: This noun refers to the blessing, prosperity, or good outcome connected with having children. It describes children as a gift and a source of family flourishing, rather than naming a specific child or describing the act of birth itself. The word appears once in the Greek LXX corpus, in 4 Maccabees 18:9. Its central sense is expressed by “blessing of children” and “breed of goodly children.” The precise force of its single use depends on the surrounding verse and passage.

word:lxx:L705850.explanation: Zachōr, also written Zakhor, is a proper name rather than a general descriptive word. In the Greek Old Testament, it occurs once, in Nehemiah 10:13, identifying a person named Zachor. The name itself does not provide a further meaning or describe an action, quality, or event in the information available here. Its precise significance in that verse depends on the surrounding passage and the person’s place in that record.

word:lxx:L705924.explanation: Ē means or, presenting an alternative.

word:lxx:L705991.explanation: This adjective describes someone or something that is partly dead, severely weakened, or close to death. The surrounding verse is needed to determine exactly who or what is described there, but the word itself points to a state of near-death and serious weakness.

word:lxx:L706024.explanation: Ērōn, rendered “Iron,” is a proper name identifying a person rather than describing a quality or action. Because the available text does not include the surrounding verse, the name itself gives no further personal description or significance. Its basic function is simply to identify this individual in that genealogical or community record.

word:lxx:L706091.explanation: Thana is a proper name, identifying a person or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L706486.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered as “Ideia” or “Ithia.” It identifies a specific person or designation rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L706518.explanation: This word is a proper name, rendered “Iebousai” or “Ievuse.” It identifies a specifically named person, people, or place rather than expressing an action, quality, or general idea. word:lxx:L706622.explanation: Ierkaan is a personal name, referring to an individual rather than describing an action, quality, or object. word:lxx:L706716.explanation: Hiketeuō means to approach as a suppliant—to beseech or supplicate someone humbly.

word:lxx:L706763.explanation: Iordanēs is the name Jordan, a place that people crossed and where they stood.

word:lxx:L706877.explanation: This word is a personal name: “Iōab” or “Ioav.” It identifies a person rather than describing an action, quality, object, or idea. word:lxx:L706899.explanation: Iōacha, also rendered Ioakha, is a personal name in the Greek Old Testament.
